title: From Chaos to Choreography: Multi-Agent Orchestration Patterns That Actually Work — Sandipan Bhaumik
talk_summary: The speaker argues multi-agent systems are distributed systems and recommends explicit coordination, immutable versioned state, data contracts, circuit breakers, compensation, and observability. He illustrates with a credit-decisioning race condition and a centralized orchestrator architecture.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use a central workflow engine/DAG that calls agents, manages parallelism/retries/state, and prevents agents from calling each other.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every call goes through the orchestrator. Agents never call each other. The orchestrator is the single source of truth.
takeaways.numbers: 5 agents create at least 10 potential connections; complexity can grow ~25x

takeaways.what_they_do: Store each agent handoff as a new append-only version with schema and creator; agents read a sealed snapshot and produce a new one.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Each agent appends a new version instead of updating the shared state.

takeaways.what_they_do: Define input/output schemas and reject handoffs that fail type/confidence checks at the boundary.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If confidence is below 0.7, it will reject the handoff.

takeaways.what_they_do: Track consecutive failures/timeouts and open circuit to fail fast, then half-open test after cooldown.
takeaways.evidence_quote: If agent B fails repeatedly, say five times in a row, the circuit breaker opens.

takeaways.what_they_do: Each agent action has execute and compensate; orchestrator tracks successes and rolls back in reverse on failure.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Every agent has two methods, execute and compensate.

takeaways.technique: Trace every handoff with state version
takeaways.what_they_do: Log each agent call, inputs/outputs, latency/token usage, and state version so event flows can be reconstructed.
takeaways.evidence_quote: You need bulletproof observability to make choreography work.
